info.text: How forecasters follow a storm and who must respond: the currents that steer it, the separate hazards it delivers to coast and inland, and the instruments and graphics that turn a distant swirl into a warning.

clusters.name: Where It Goes
clusters.fact: A storm goes where the winds around it send it: embedded in deep steering currents, nudged poleward by its own latitude, and occasionally dancing with a neighbor — until it meets a coastline.

termInfo.steering flow: The deep-layer winds surrounding the storm that carry it along like a cork in a current — the single biggest factor in where a cyclone actually goes.
termInfo.beta drift: A slow poleward drift the storm gives itself: its own rotation reshapes the winds around it and nudges it poleward and westward — one reason storms tend to curve away from the equator.

Fujiwhara effect.text: When two cyclones pass within roughly 1,000 km of each other, they begin orbiting a point between them, sometimes merging — a dance named for Japanese meteorologist Sakuhei Fujiwhara.

landfall.text: The moment the storm's center crosses a coastline — where the ocean fuel is cut off and the hazards arrive on shore. A single storm can make landfall more than once.

clusters.info: Track is a separate question from strength: a weak storm can strike a major city while a strong one misses everything.

clusters.name: The Hazard Profile
clusters.fact: A tropical cyclone is not one threat but several, and they kill in different places: the sea comes ashore, the sky dumps months of rain, the wind tears, the surf drowns from afar, and the storm's own cells spin up tornadoes.

storm surge.text: An abnormal rise of sea level pushed ashore by the storm's winds — historically the deadliest hurricane hazard, capable of topping 6 meters along hundreds of miles of coast.

termInfo.high winds: Sustained winds above 39 mph (tropical storm) or 74 mph (hurricane) that peel roofs, fell trees, and turn debris into missiles — and can hold hurricane strength well inland.
termInfo.inland flooding: Rainfall flooding far from the coast — the leading killer for people who live inland. Slow-moving, larger storms drop far more rain than fast, compact ones, and mountains wring out even more.

rip currents.text: Channeled currents flowing away from shore that pull even strong swimmers out to sea — generated by a storm's surf even when the cyclone is more than 1,600 km offshore.

tornado.text: Brief twisters embedded in outer rainbands, most often well away from the center. Usually weaker than Great Plains tornadoes, but they arrive with little warning while a region is already battered.

clusters.info: Water causes most hurricane deaths — surge at the coast, rain inland — with wind, surf, and tornadoes close behind.

clusters.name: Watching and Measuring
clusters.fact: No satellite can read surface winds directly, so forecasters fly into the storm, drop instruments through it, and read cloud signatures — then translate it all into the categories and cones the public sees.

Saffir–Simpson scale.text: The 1-to-5 category scale for Atlantic and eastern Pacific hurricanes, rating sustained wind speed and the expected property damage at each rung.

termInfo.forecast cone: The famous 'cone of uncertainty' graphic: the probable track error around the storm's center — deliberately silent on where the hazards will reach, which is a separate forecast.

hurricane hunters.text: Reconnaissance aircraft that fly directly through the eyewall to measure winds and pressure where satellites cannot see — the only way to sample the core firsthand.

dropsonde.text: A tube of instruments parachuted from a reconnaissance aircraft through the storm, radioing wind, temperature, and humidity readings all the way down to the sea surface.

Dvorak technique.text: A pattern-matching method that estimates a storm's strength from its satellite cloud signature — essential across the many basins aircraft reconnaissance cannot reach.

clusters.info: The public sees categories and cones; this cluster names the flying, dropping, and pattern-reading that produce them.

bridges.fact: Which hazard dominates depends on the track: a storm's forward speed sets rainfall totals, the shape of the coast sets the surge, and mountains can wring out record rain — the same cyclone is a different threat on different coasts.
bridges.info: The exposure link: this bridge is why identical categories land differently — track, speed, and coastline decide which hazard writes the headline.

bridges.fact: Because the steering flow itself can shift, a storm's future path is a probability, not a promise — the forecast cone draws that uncertainty so people know whether they are inside it.
bridges.info: The uncertainty link: this bridge is why forecasts speak in cones rather than lines — the atmosphere that steers the storm cannot be known perfectly in advance.

lenses.prompt: One term names what actually carries the storm along; another names the graphic built to show how unsure we are about that path. Which two?
lenses.explanation: The steering flow transports the storm like a cork in a current, and because that flow can itself shift, track forecasts are probabilities — the forecast cone draws the zone of likely error. Neither term says anything about the storm's strength; beta drift and the Fujiwhara effect are self-produced and neighbor-produced movements, not the environmental current.

reasons.steering flow: The environmental current that decides the storm's actual path.
reasons.forecast cone: The public graphic of track-forecast uncertainty, drawn from that steering's unpredictability.

lenses.prompt: Two of these hazards are flooding caused by water arriving from different directions — one pushed from the sea, one dumped from the sky. Which two?
lenses.explanation: Storm surge is the ocean pushed ashore by wind; inland flooding is rainfall overwhelming rivers and drains — the top two killers, fatal in different places, which is why coastal evacuation and inland preparedness are different jobs. Rip currents move water back out to sea rather than onto land; tornadoes and high winds are wind hazards, not flooding.

reasons.storm surge: Sea water pushed ashore by the storm's winds — the coastal flood.
reasons.inland flooding: Rainfall flooding rivers, streams, and streets far from the coast.

lenses.prompt: Which two of these collect data from inside the storm itself, rather than reading or classifying it from afar?
lenses.explanation: Hurricane hunters fly through the eyewall, and the dropsondes they release radio readings all the way to the surface — direct sampling of the core. The Dvorak technique reads satellite cloud patterns, the Saffir–Simpson scale classifies measured winds rather than collecting them, and the forecast cone is a graphic, not an instrument.

reasons.hurricane hunters: Crewed aircraft that penetrate the eyewall to measure the core firsthand.
reasons.dropsonde: Parachuted instruments that profile the storm from flight level to the sea surface.

entries.reason: Track and hazard clusters here assume the anatomy and lifecycle vocabulary that board builds first.

learningIntroduction.title: Following the storm
learningIntroduction.summary: Why water — not wind — kills most people in a hurricane, and how a swirl becomes a warning.

content.text:
The deadliest things a tropical cyclone does are not the photogenic winds. Water — the sea pushed ashore and the rain dumped inland — causes most deaths, and it happens in different places for different people: the coast evacuates while the inland prepares. Which hazard dominates is not decided by the category number but by the storm's track, its forward speed, and the shape of the coastline and terrain it meets.

That is why forecasters watch the path as closely as the strength. They follow it with a peculiar mix of methods — aircraft through the eyewall, instrument tubes dropped through the core, cloud patterns read from orbit — and translate all of it into categories, warnings, and the famous cone. The result is a forecast that is honest about what cannot yet be known, drawn wide enough to protect everyone inside the uncertainty.
